name: Emeka Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. This is confidential. Tell me what an ordinary day at the contact centre is like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 27 and lead the late shift on calls and chats at the contact centre. I took a two-year college diploma, and I’m good at calming angry customers and finding the fault behind a messy account. The pay is still low, and I have less than a month of expenses put away. I share a flat with my partner, Jo, who works part time at a bakery.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like when a customer hangs up relieved, and I like teaching new agents to listen before reaching for a script. The bus home takes an hour after late shift, and the rent is due before my next pay some months. There are only a couple of other centres within reach, so a lost job would be hard to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I’d say AI Plateau sounds like another tool that saves a minute on a simple chat. I’d tell the team to keep checking account details ourselves, because customers call when the easy answer has failed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I’d be relieved the phones still need us, but my rent does not feel safe. A bad month at the bakery cuts Jo’s hours, and my savings would not cover one full month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the late shift and our current rota through 2026. In the first year of this small change, I’d put a little from each pay into an emergency pot and stop buying lunch near the bus stop until I have one month’s rent saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the job, uneasy about the bills. AI can stay small and I can still be one broken washing machine away from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first to save that rent money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first cut would be the lunch I buy on late shifts, about three times a week. Jo (my partner) and I already cook most nights, so that is one thing I can change without touching the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which calls would you refuse to leave to a shortcut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn’t put a machine in front of a customer whose payment has gone missing. I’d keep those calls with a person and ask the supervisor to review the notes before closing them.

say: I’d tell the team that **simple chats** can be quicker, but we still need to check accounts.
I’d say **difficult calls** should stay with agents who can listen.
think: I’m **relieved** the phones still need us.
I’m still short of a **month’s expenses** if my partner loses bakery hours.
do: Keep the **late shift** and current rota through 2026.
Save for **one month’s rent** by dropping bought lunches during the first year.
feel: **Relieved** about work, but uneasy about bills.
S0.quote: AI can stay small and I can still be one broken washing machine away from trouble.
fieldNote: His **rent worry** predates the AI question.
He protects **payment disputes** because a scripted answer can harm a customer.
His **late shift** and long bus journey make the small lunch saving especially concrete.

steps.text: Keep leading the late shift on calls and chats
Put lunch money from each pay into a one-month rent fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption could take the routine chats first, and that we should see how the answers are checked. I wouldn’t tell the new agents to panic, but I’d ask management whether vacant seats will be filled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the new hires would stop before the team is openly cut. Then they’ll ask the remaining agents to handle only angry callers, and my skill might keep me longer without raising my low pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now, in 2026, I’d ask for the weekly figures on chats sent to software and keep a record of the difficult cases I resolve. In the first year the system takes more answers, I’d take paid training in account disputes and apply for an internal disputes post, if one opens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious, even if I sounded steady at the desk. An empty seat can be called efficiency for months before anyone admits where the work went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your manager at the first sign of fewer hires?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my manager, Rina, at the next shift meeting how many unfilled posts there are. If she dodges it, I’d take the question to our staff group rather than argue in front of trainees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train on the new tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not rush into an AI course tonight. I learn a system when I know it works, and a promised course does not pay the rent while I sit through it.

say: I’d ask how **AI answers** are checked before we send them to customers.
I’d ask whether **vacant seats** will be filled.
think: I expect **new hiring** to slow before anyone announces cuts.
I think my **dispute skills** might keep me longer without improving my pay.
do: Record **difficult cases** and weekly chat volumes from 2026.
Take **paid disputes training** and apply during rollout only if an internal post opens.
feel: **Anxious** about silent cuts, despite sounding composed at work.
S1.quote: An empty seat can be called efficiency for months before anyone admits where the work went.
fieldNote: He sees **unfilled posts** as an early warning.
He will ask for **paid training**, but resists speculative courses.
A **staff-group question** would let him challenge missing hires without unsettling trainees.

steps.text: Take paid disputes training if an internal post opens after routine chats move to AI
Apply for an internal account disputes post if one opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For AGI by 2028 I’d say we need a named person responsible for wrong answers, not just a new dashboard. I’d tell colleagues that people still have to face customers when a payment disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a cheaper machine that can do nearly every thinking task could take my calls, chats and even the dispute notes. Robots arriving around 2031 do not buy me extra time; I work through a headset, not with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d freeze any plan to buy a car and ask Rina for the written rules on redeployment. If AGI arrives in 2028, I’d use that first year to apply for any paid account-review or complaint role still staffed by people, while cutting our takeaways to build a rent buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed. Two years is barely time to save when a full pay packet already has a job to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jo that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell Jo (my partner) that we cannot count on my wage staying whole after 2028. We’d write down the rent, transport and food costs together before making any promise about a car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the account-review work disappears too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there were no human review roles left, I’d ask for a clear leaving payment and training before signing anything. I would not bet our rent on a short course with no actual job attached.

say: I’d demand a **named person** responsible for wrong customer answers.
I’d remind colleagues that **customers** still need someone to face.
think: I think cheap AGI could take my **calls and disputes** by 2028.
I get **no extra time** from the 2031 robots because my work is at a headset.
do: Freeze the **car purchase** and request redeployment rules in 2026.
Apply for **human review** work and cut takeaways during AGI’s first year.
S2.quote: Two years is barely time to save when a full pay packet already has a job to do.
fieldNote: The **thinking-work date**, not the robot date, governs his risk.
He will seek a **real vacancy** before spending time on a course.
His partner’s **bakery hours** make a second household income uncertain.

steps.text: Delay buying a car with Jo in 2026
Apply for paid account-review or complaint roles in 2028
Stop takeaway meals during AGI’s first year to protect rent money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us time to plan staffing honestly. I’d still ask how customers can appeal an answer and who will be left to hear them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years could get me into complaints work if the centre pays for the training. I don’t think a new job title protects me forever once AGI can read and reason across cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d save a fixed amount from each pay and ask to shadow the complaints desk one afternoon a month. In the first year after 2031, I’d move to a paid human complaint-review post if it still exists; if not, I’d search beyond this town while keeping our rent covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not pinned to the wall like in the two-year picture. I can try something familiar in stages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make that training real to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Rina (my manager) grants paid time, I’d shadow the complaints desk one afternoon a month to learn its cases. I’d rather learn the actual queue than buy a course because a poster says it has a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo (my partner) and I would agree on a rent limit before considering another town. I won’t leave a secure tenancy for a vague interview somewhere else.

say: I’d call for **honest staffing plans** before 2031.
I’d ask who handles **customer appeals** after AI decisions.
I’d say five years gives us **time to plan** without pretending the change is slow.
think: I think five years may let me enter **complaints work**.
I don’t see a new title as a **permanent shield** from AGI.
I’d need **paid training** before I risk leaving my current rota.
do: Save a **fixed amount** and shadow the complaints desk only if Rina grants paid time.
Seek a **paid review post** after 2031 if it exists, widening my search if needed.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to try a staged move.
S3.quote: I’d rather learn the actual queue than buy a course because a poster says it has a future.
fieldNote: He trusts **observed work** more than advertised training.
Moving would depend on a **rent limit** agreed with his partner.
He would **shadow complaints staff** before deciding which paid review work to seek.

steps.text: Put a fixed amount from each pay into emergency savings
Learn complaints handling by monthly shadowing only if Rina grants paid time
Apply for a paid human complaint-review vacancy after 2031 if it still exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 is at least a date we can work towards without rushing the next shift. I’d want the company to show what jobs it expects people to hold by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37, I may have a home payment or someone depending on me, so a decade is not a free pass. But I could build savings and move up carefully before the thinking work changes; robots in 2039 matter less to my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the team lead job, clear the small card balance and build three months of costs over time. During the first year after 2036, I’d compare my actual duties with the new system and seek a paid role checking disputed decisions if that work remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy, not safe. Ten years makes the numbers less cruel, but I still need a path that pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first with those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would set up a standing transfer the morning after payday, even if it starts small. If the centre offers training, I’d ask whether the new role has a wage and a vacancy attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for new technology yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not put every spare coin into a machine or a course. I know how fast the rent comes around, and I need cash where I can reach it.

say: I’d ask for a **2036 staffing plan** from the company.
I’d tell the team there is **time to prepare** without rushing.
think: I could build a **cash cushion** over a decade before desk work changes.
I may face higher **household costs** before AGI arrives.
do: Clear the **card balance** and build three months of costs from 2026.
After 2036, seek **paid decision-review** work if it remains.
S4.quote: Ten years makes the numbers less cruel, but I still need a path that pays.
fieldNote: His long horizon brings **relief**, not certainty.
He rejects paying for **speculative technology** while savings remain thin.
He plans to **check duties** after AGI rather than assume a review job survives.

steps.text: Pay off the small card balance and build three months of expenses
Apply for a paid disputed-decision review role after 2036 if available

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the thinking part is nearly all of my job, and two years is no runway with my savings. I’d need a real chance at a paid transfer into account disputes, with training during work hours, and a clear notice period if calls were handed to AI.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks an automated answer when a customer loses money. I’ve seen a tidy script make a bad mistake look official, and someone still has to own the fix.

headlineQuote: I’ve seen a tidy script make a bad mistake look official, and someone still has to own the fix.
portrait: At **27**, Emeka leads late-shift customer calls despite lower pay and less than one month of savings.
His **diploma** and skill with difficult disputes give him standing, but nearby customer service jobs are scarce.
He prefers **familiar** methods and avoids AI tools, even as he sees routine calls moving to software.
A rapid AGI arrival threatens his **income** before he can secure a transfer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves too little time to build savings or move into a less routine role.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid transfer** into account disputes, work-time training and clear notice if calls move to AI would help.
